title: Youll Figure it Out
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article makes the case for deliberate leader non-involvement as a development tool, arguing that swooping in to help solve a hard problem robs team members of the chance to build mastery and self-reliance. The phrase 'You'll figure it out,' delivered with genuine confidence rather than dismissiveness, is presented as a powerful signal of trust that pushes people to rise to a challenge they didn't think they could meet. The piece acknowledges this is uncomfortable for many leaders to do, but frames stepping back — while still projecting confidence in the team's ability — as how initiative and creativity actually get built.
points: Leader non-involvement is framed as an active development choice, not passivity — withholding help is what forces the growth that direct assistance would prevent.
The specific phrase matters: 'You'll figure it out' works because it signals genuine confidence, distinguishing it from dismissiveness or abandonment.
The article names the emotional cost directly — it's uncomfortable for leaders to stay out of the way — while arguing that discomfort is the price of building real initiative.
quotes: Leaders who swoop in and assist team members in solving the problem miss a critical opportunity to develop and grow mastery in those they lead.

When those who are now responsible for solving the problem bemoan that they have no idea how to navigate the challenge, a great leader will sometimes say, “You’ll figure it out,” and then walk away with a mischievous grin.
By avoiding getting involved and helping others address the problem, good leaders also promote the creativity and the self-reliance that is so critical to independent thinking.
Giving team members the autonomy to wrestle with a difficult problem while at the same time instilling them with confidence is how people learn, grow, and develop.
People are at their most creative when solving a gnarly problem a leader believes they can. So, good leaders leave them alone to do it.
